newsitem.title: USA: Senator vows legislation to curb mortgage insurance.
newsitem.headline: Senator vows legislation to curb mortgage insurance.

text.p: Senate Banking Committee chairman Alfonse D'Amato vowed Wednesday to move forward on legislation to prevent insurers from charging homeowners for unneccessary mortgage insurance policies.
The bill, which passed the House of Representatives in April on a 421 to 7 vote, has been held up in the Senate by some Republicans who have voiced objections from the insurance industry.
D'Amato had been seeking a compromise approach that would be acceptable to all parties, but at a hearing on lending disclosure laws, the New York Republican said his patience was wearing thin.
"To my colleagues, I say to you, Alfonse has not stopped," D'Amato said. "I will at an appropriate time bring an amendment on the floor."
D'Amato said he would seek an opportunity to attach the private mortgage insurance restrictions to unrelated, popular legislation in order to force a vote.
The bill passed by the House, H.R. 607, known as the Homeowners Insurance Protection Act, would allow homeowners to cancel mortgage insurance when they build up sufficient equity.

Currently, mortgage lenders require a borrower to obtain and pay for such insurance when the borrower is making a relatively small down payment, such as 5 percent of the purchase price of a home. Borrowers putting down 20 percent or more generally are not required to obtain insurance, which can cost $300 to $900 a year.
Homeowners who build up 20 percent or more equity are generally allowed to opt out of mortgage insurance, but insurers sometimes fail to notify borrowers that they can cancel the policy.

In some cases, insurance companies resisted borrowers' attempts to cancel. Representative James Hansen (R-Utah), who authored the House bill, spent several years convincing one company to cancel unneeded insurance on an apartment he owned near Washington, D.C.

The House bill would automatically cancel a mortgage insurance policy if the homeowner was current on mortgage payments and had built up equity equal to 25 percent of the original value of the house. Homeowner's equity is the value of the home after subtracting the remaining principal on a mortgage.
Mortgage insurance companies oppose the House bill, which they say would escalate the cost of mortgages by imposing unnecessary government controls.
Consumer advocates, who strongly back the bill, said borrowers are losing millions of dollars a year by continuing to pay for insurance after building up sufficient equity.
Proponents of the measure feared that the bill might die in the Senate after D'Amato's committee in April postponed a planned vote.
D'Amato said Wednesday he would move the legislation one way or another. "We can do it the nice way or we can do it a way some of my colleagues will not enjoy," he said.
